title: The chapter of eights
hook: sixteen short poems against clinging to views

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nalaka, the half-full pot and the full lake, and your line, what is full is quiet. Did you let one pause stay a pause? Today we step into the Sutta Nipata's fourth chapter. Day six hundred seven.

An argument online: two people, each certain, each quoting, each getting louder. Neither one changes the other's mind, and both log off a little more sure they were right. There's a set of old poems that looks at that exact scene and asks a strange question. Not who's right. But what happens to a person who needs to be. That's the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata, sixteen short poems with a curious name. Today: the Atthakavagga, the chapter of eights.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, EACH CERTAIN.` → `NOT WHO'S RIGHT.` → `WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ONE WHO NEEDS TO BE?`

segments.voice: Atthaka means a group of eight, and vagga means a chapter. The name probably comes from several of its poems that have eight verses each: the eights on the cave, on the corrupted, on the pure, on the supreme. Not all sixteen do. Some scholars count this chapter among the early layers of Buddhist verse, partly because other parts of the canon know it by name. In the Udana, a monk named Sona is invited to recite, and he chants all sixteen poems of the eights from memory; the Buddha praises how well he has learned them. In that story, the poems are already a set, known by heart. What do the poems say? Again and again, the same thing from different sides. People hold a view and call it the best. They call everyone else's foolish. They go into the assembly to argue, hungry for praise, and if they lose they're stung. The sage, the poems say, doesn't step into that ring. Not because he has a cleverer view, but because he doesn't grasp any view as the thing that makes him pure. Some of the lines are hard and some teachers read them in different ways: does the sage hold no views at all, or holds them lightly? The poems themselves leave room for both.
screen: `ATTHAKA: A GROUP OF EIGHT.` · `KNOWN BY NAME ELSEWHERE.` · `SONA CHANTS THEM FROM MEMORY.` · `THE SAGE DOESN'T ENTER THE RING.` · then, large: `NO VIEW TO CLING TO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one poem, tonight, slowly, the way Sona would have heard it. For now, sit and settle. Bring to mind one opinion you hold strongly. Not to drop it. Just notice how it sits in the body when you think of someone who disagrees: the jaw, the chest, the hands. Notice the wanting to win. Then let the breath soften that place, and let the opinion simply be an opinion, held in an open hand. The bell holds the time.
Atthakavagga. The chapter of eights, the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata: sixteen short, old poems on not clinging to views. Today's word.
Your line: no view to cling to. Today, when you feel the need to win a point, try asking one real question instead, and listen to the answer. Day six hundred seven.

howItsDone: The Atthakavagga is studied in Theravada monasteries and widely read by lay Buddhists and scholars for its early style; teachers often draw on it when speaking about letting go of attachment to views.

fork.setup: two teachers are debating in the assembly, each calling his own view the purest. you're the sage the Atthakavagga describes. what do you do?
options: join in with a better argument.
stay out of it, holding no view as what makes you pure.
fork.reveal: the poems' sage doesn't step into the dispute; it's grasping at a view as purifying that he lets go of.

original.note: Pali atthakavagga: the chapter of eights, the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata.

trapdoor: what you thought: the chapter of eights has eight poems.
what it means: it has sixteen; several have eight verses each, and all warn against clinging to views.
what a scholar hears: the Atthakavagga is quoted elsewhere in the canon (Sona's recital in Udana 5.6; Mahakaccana explaining a verse in SN 22.3), which is one reason some scholars date it early.

notes: Sn 4 paraphrased. Confirm which suttas carry atthaka in their names (Guhatthaka, Dutthatthaka, Suddhatthaka, Paramatthaka) and the explanation of the chapter's name.
'Many scholars think this chapter is among the oldest layers' is a scholarly consensus claim; confirm wording. The Chinese parallel is the Arthapada Sutra (Taisho 198); confirm.
The practice turns 'read one poem' into a sit, with the reading suggested for later; a Keeper may want to name a specific poem to read (e.g. Sn 4.8 or 4.12).
Whether the sage holds no views or holds them lightly is debated among teachers and scholars; the script names both readings without choosing.
